name: Modality effect
statement: Words that are heard are recalled better than words that are read, and the advantage is confined to the last item or two of a list.
meaning: Present a list one word at a time and test recall at once. Recall of the final position is higher when the words were spoken than when they were shown on a screen. The gap is large at the end of the list and absent in the middle. Early positions often run the other way, with silent reading beating listening, which the literature calls the inverse modality effect. For about two decades the auditory advantage was read as a readout from an echo, a brief store holding sound after the sound has stopped. That explanation was abandoned and the effect stayed. A second and unrelated claim travels under the same name in education research, that a diagram is learned better with spoken narration than with on-screen text. This entry is about the memory finding, and it keeps the teaching claim separate, because the two rest on different evidence and report different sizes.

origin.who: Bennet B. Murdock Jr and Keith D. Walker
origin.where: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
origin.note: Their free-recall paper is the one the free-recall literature cites for the effect. It is paywalled, and its record was verified at Crossref rather than read, so what appears here about it is taken from later papers that describe it. Conrad and Hull had published the same asymmetry for serial recall a year earlier in Psychonomic Science. Crowder and Morton's precategorical acoustic storage paper, which supplied the explanation the effect carried for a decade, appeared in the same year as Murdock and Walker.

evidence: Roediger and Crowder set out the three findings the sensory-echo account rested on: the auditory advantage for the last few items of a list, the suffix effect, and the partial-report advantage in multichannel listening. Their experiment tested the second. 160 Yale undergraduates heard 16 lists of 12 words at one word a second, with half the lists followed by the spoken word 'Recall' and half by two tones. Averaged over serial positions 7 to 12, the spoken cue cost .10 of the proportion recalled under serial-recall instructions, .09 under free recall, .09 under free position recall, and .04 when subjects were told to recall the last few items first. The same suffix raised recall of the first three positions under the two order-based instructions. The near-equality across the four instruction types was the problem the authors named: the conditions imposed different delays between the last word and its recall, and a store thought to last about two seconds should have produced suffix effects of different sizes. Grenfell-Essam, Ward and Tan then ran the comparison across tasks. Forty students at Essex in each of two experiments took lists of two to twelve words, for either immediate free recall or immediate serial recall. The auditory advantage appeared in both tasks at every list length except two words. On short lists it was large and limited to the final serial position, the shape Conrad and Hull had reported for serial recall. On longer lists it was smaller and spread back over the last two or three positions, the shape reported for free recall. Visual advantages appeared at early positions on the longer lists in both tasks. Comparing the magnitude of performance for the two tasks at matched list lengths and serial positions gave r(44) = 0.858 in the first experiment. It gave 0.709 in the second, where the spoken condition was reading each word aloud rather than listening.

replication.headline: Pazdera and Kahana tested 1,469 people online with presentation modality varied between subjects, and found the auditory advantage at the end of the list and the visual advantage at the start of it in the same data.
replication.detail: Experiment 2 assigned 735 participants to visual presentation and 734 to auditory, with lists of 12 and 24 words at two presentation rates. Mixed effects logistic regressions were fitted to the proportion recalled from the last five and the first three positions. Modality had a main effect on recency performance, chi-square(1) = 114.60, p < .001, and on primacy performance, chi-square(1) = 11.63, p < .001. The second effect ran in the visual direction. Experiment 1 varied modality within subjects across 888 participants and gave chi-square(1) = 189.68 for recency and 97.54 for primacy, both p < .001. No interaction of modality with list length or with presentation rate reached significance in either experiment. The authors then fitted the Context Maintenance and Retrieval model and reproduced both effects by letting temporal context drift faster and context-to-item associations form more strongly under auditory presentation, with no separate store for recent items. Text and figures were read from the accepted manuscript posted by the Computational Memory Lab, which its own first page says may not exactly match the published version.

study.cite: Pazdera, J. K., & Kahana, M. J. (2023). Modality effects in free recall: A retrieved-context account. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 49(6), 866-888.

limits: No effect size appears above because none of the papers read here reports one for the modality effect. They report proportion recalled by serial position, chi-squares and F ratios, so the structured effect-size fields are left empty. The effect has edges. Grenfell-Essam and colleagues found none at a list length of two words. Beaman obtained a visual advantage in serial recall by requiring recall of the list in two sections, and describes it, judged list-wide, as equivalent in size to the classical auditory advantage. The education claim is a separate literature with a separate record. Ginns applied meta-analysis to 43 independent effects, 39 of them between-subjects and four within-subjects. The ERIC record of that paper was read and states no effect size, so the figure of d = 0.72 attached to it here is taken from Reinwein's abstract and not from Ginns. Reinwein redid the analysis on 86 independent effects and reports d = 0.38, falling to d = 0.20 after Duval and Tweedie trim and fill for publication bias. Murdock and Walker, Crowder and Morton, Penney, Gardiner and Gregg, and Glenberg were all paywalled. What appears here about them is read from Crossref records, from PubMed abstracts, and from the review sections of Pazdera and Kahana and of Roediger and Crowder, and it is attributed in each case. Searches covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, ERIC and web search, and no meta-analysis of the memory version of the effect was located.
misreadings: The echo is the first error. Crowder and Morton proposed a precategorical acoustic store holding sound briefly after it stops, and textbook accounts still explain the modality effect by it and quote a duration of about two seconds. Crowder wrote in 1979 that the two-second estimate was 'pure conjecture, and there was then no evidence (nor is there now) to prefer it over some other figure of the same order of magnitude', and that it had become the paper's most cited statement. The evidence went past the number. Huang and Glenberg define a long-term modality effect, an auditory advantage for the last list item that survives a filled retention interval. They report that a redundant auditory suffix produced no reliable reduction in recall of that item, which an echoic account predicts it should. Roediger and Crowder had already found the suffix effect to be about the same size under instructions that changed how long the last items waited before recall. The second error is that the effect needs sound. Pazdera and Kahana's review lists it for vocalised reading, silent mouthing, lip reading, sign language and finger spelling, each with its own citations, none of which were read here. Grenfell-Essam and colleagues obtained the effect in their second experiment with reading aloud as the spoken condition. The third error is direction. Hearing does not beat reading across the board. The advantage sits at the end of the list, and early positions can favour silent reading, which Pazdera and Kahana found in both their experiments and Grenfell-Essam and colleagues found at early positions on longer lists. The fourth error is the name. Education research uses modality effect for the claim that a diagram is learned better with narration than with on-screen text. Ginns's meta-analysis of that claim covered 43 independent effects, Reinwein's covered 86 and roughly halved the estimate, and correcting for publication bias halved it again. Reinwein also argues that the teaching effect cannot rest on Penney's separate-streams model or on Baddeley's working memory. A page that cites Murdock and Walker in support of a rule about slide design has joined two literatures that do not report the same size of effect.

sources.text: Murdock, B. B., Jr., & Walker, K. D. (1969). Modality effects in free recall. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 8(5), 665-676. Paywalled; the record was verified at Crossref and the paper is described here only as later papers describe it.

Conrad, R., & Hull, A. J. (1968). Input modality and the serial position curve in short-term memory. Psychonomic Science, 10(4), 135-136. Named as the serial-recall antecedent on the strength of Grenfell-Essam, Ward and Tan's description; not read.
Crowder, R. G., & Morton, J. (1969). Precategorical acoustic storage (PAS). Perception & Psychophysics, 5(6), 365-373. Paywalled; the record was verified at Crossref.

Crowder, R. G. (1979). This Week's Citation Classic: commentary on Crowder & Morton (1969), dated 17 April 1979 and published in the issue of 19 November 1979. Read in full from the scan in the Garfield library at the University of Pennsylvania; the source of the quoted remark that the two-second estimate was pure conjecture.

Roediger, H. L., III, & Crowder, R. G. (1976). Recall instructions and the suffix effect. The American Journal of Psychology, 89(1), 115-125. Read in full from the scan hosted by the Washington University memory lab.

Grenfell-Essam, R., Ward, G., & Tan, L. (2017). Common modality effects in immediate free recall and immediate serial recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 43(12), 1909-1933. Read in full from the Europe PMC author manuscript.

Pazdera, J. K., & Kahana, M. J. (2023). Modality effects in free recall: A retrieved-context account. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 49(6), 866-888. Read in full from the accepted manuscript posted by the Computational Memory Lab.

Huang, S.-T., & Glenberg, A. M. (1986). Echoic and retrieval accounts of the long-term modality effect tested using the suffix procedure. The American Journal of Psychology, 99(4), 453-470. Read from its PubMed abstract.
Beaman, C. P. (2002). Inverting the modality effect in serial recall. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology Section A, 55(2), 371-389. Read from its PubMed abstract.

Penney, C. G. (1989). Modality effects and the structure of short-term verbal memory. Memory & Cognition, 17(4), 398-422. Paywalled; read from its PubMed abstract, which is the source for the separate-streams description.

Ginns, P. (2005). Meta-analysis of the modality effect. Learning and Instruction, 15(4), 313-331. Paywalled; the ERIC record was read for the counts of independent effects, and it prints no effect size.

Reinwein, J. (2012). Does the modality effect exist? And if so, which modality effect? Journal of Psycholinguistic Research, 41(1), 1-32. Read from its PubMed abstract, which is the source for both its own figures and for the d = 0.72 attributed to Ginns.

Gardiner, J. M., & Gregg, V. H. (1979). When auditory memory is not overwritten. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 18(6), 705-719. Named as a source of the long-term modality effect on the strength of Pazdera and Kahana's review; not read.

Glenberg, A. M. (1984). A retrieval account of the long-term modality effect. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 10(1), 16-31. Named on the strength of Pazdera and Kahana's review; not read.

Campbell, R., & Dodd, B. (1980). Hearing by eye. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 32(1), 85-99. Cited by Pazdera and Kahana for lip-read modality and suffix effects; the PubMed record carries no abstract and the paper was not read.
